blocks.text: A **queue** is a line. New items join at one end, the **back**, and items leave from the other end, the **front** — in exactly the order they arrived. Whoever has waited longest is served next. That rule has a name: **FIFO** — **first in, first out**.

blocks.alt: A queue of four people: Ann at the front, then Bob, Cat and Dan at the back. Ann, who arrived first, is the next to leave from the front. A new person, Eve, joins at the back, behind Dan.
blocks.caption: Whoever has waited longest is served next.

blocks.text: Think of a line at a ticket counter
Nobody pushes in at the front, and nobody is served from the middle. You join at the back and wait your turn. A queue in programming follows the same rules, with five operations:

items: **dequeue()** — remove the item at the **front** and return it.
**peek()** (also called **front**) — look at the front item without removing it.

blocks.text: Each one is **O(1)**: enqueue only ever touches the back, and dequeue only the front, however long the line gets.
Enqueue 10, 20 and 30, then dequeue: you get **10** back — the first one in. The order items go in is exactly the order they come out.

blocks.alt: Six snapshots of one queue. Start empty. Enqueue 10. Enqueue 20. Enqueue 30, which joins at the back. Dequeue returns 10, the first one in, leaving 20 and 30 with 20 at the front. Peek returns 20 and changes nothing.

blocks.text: Try your own sequence. Dequeue always serves whoever joined **earliest**.

blocks.caption: Type operations like enqueue 5, dequeue, peek, size — then step through them.

blocks.text: Wrap the storage in a class with these five methods and the rule can't be broken by accident. Python, Java and C++ have a fast double-ended list built in to store the items. JavaScript doesn't — and `shift()`, which removes an array's first item, moves every other item down one place. So the JavaScript version keeps a `head` index instead: dequeue just moves it one step on.
Each language reports an empty dequeue its own way — `undefined`, `None`, `null` or an exception — but the meaning is the same: nobody was waiting.
A **stack** is the queue's twin with the opposite rule: items are added and removed at the **same** end, so the newest leaves first — **last in, first out** (LIFO). Same items in, opposite order out:

blocks.alt: Left: a queue with 1, 2, 3 joined in that order; the first to leave is 1, from the front. Right: a stack with 1, 2, 3 pushed in that order; the first to leave is 3, from the top.

blocks.text: Choosing between them is often the first decision in a problem: does the **oldest** item matter most (queue), or the **newest** (stack)?

items: **Underflow** — dequeue or peek on an **empty** queue. There is nothing to return, so the code must check first (or report it, as above).

**Overflow** — enqueue into a queue with a **fixed capacity** that is already full. Queues that grow (like the ones above) only overflow when memory runs out; fixed-size ones, common in hardware and operating systems, must refuse the item or overwrite the oldest one.
**Front** (or head) — where items leave. **Back** (or rear, or tail) — where items join.
**enqueue** is also called **offer**, **add**, **push** or **append**, depending on the language.
**FIFO** — first in, first out. **LIFO** — last in, first out (a stack).
A queue adds at the **back** and removes from the **front**: first in, first out.
enqueue, dequeue, peek, isEmpty and size are all **O(1)**.
Dequeue or peek on an empty queue is **underflow**; enqueue into a full fixed-size queue is **overflow**.
In JavaScript, avoid `shift()` for big queues — keep a front index instead.
